stops.name: Carthage, the Byrsa hill
stops.campa: In the year the Romans and Carthaginians grind against each other in Sicily, a son is born to Hamilcar of the house of Barca, the Thunderbolt. They name him Hannibal: the Grace of Baal. The city climbs the Byrsa in white terraces above its double harbor; the sign of Tanit stands on ten thousand stelae; Melqart of Tyre keeps the sea-gates. The child opens his eyes on a city at war, and the war will never once let go of him.

stops.name: The Tophet of Salammbô, the altar of Baal Hammon
stops.campa: Hamilcar, about to sail for Iberia, sacrifices to Baal Hammon and Tanit for a fair crossing. The victim burns; the omens are good. His son, nine years old, comes to the altar and begs, with a boy's coaxing, to be taken along. Hamilcar takes the child by the right hand, leads him up to the fire, and bids him lay his palm upon the sacrifice and swear. Hannibal swears. The flame takes the words, and the words take the man: the whole war to come is lit here, at this altar, in this small burning hand.
stops.quote: I swear that I will never be a friend to the Romans.
stops.quote_source: The oath as Hannibal himself recounted it to King Antiochus, Polybius 3.11; Livy 21.1; Nepos, Hannibal 2

stops.name: The harbors of Carthage, sailing for Iberia
stops.campa: From the round war-harbor, the Cothon, whose hidden sheds hold two hundred keels, Hamilcar's fleet stands out to sea. The boy who swore rides at his father's side. Carthage has lost Sicily and Sardinia and paid the indemnity of a defeated city; Hamilcar sails to build a new empire out of Iberian silver with which to pay Rome, and one day to fight her. Hannibal watches the Byrsa sink under the horizon. He will not see it again for thirty-six years.

stops.name: Gades, the temple of Melqart at the Pillars
stops.campa: Landfall at Gades, oldest daughter of Tyre in the west, on her island at the edge of the world. Hamilcar sacrifices in the temple of Melqart, where an undying fire burns before a god who has no image, and barefoot priests in linen serve the emptiness. Beyond the temple there is only Ocean. The boy stands between the bronze pillars and learns the shape of his house's faith: the god of Tyre walks with the Barcids, west of everything.

stops.name: Akra Leuke, the white citadel
stops.campa: Hamilcar founds his white fortress above the sea and the boy grows up inside an army. Hannibal learns Iberian and Greek, the sarissa and the javelin, hunger and watch-keeping. The portrait the canon paints is formed here: first into the fight, last out of it; sleeping on the bare ground in a soldier's cloak among the sentries; eating what the ranks eat; on horse or foot beyond all others. The camp is his school, his father the only master.

stops.name: Helike, the death of Hamilcar
stops.campa: Besieging Helike in winter, Hamilcar is caught by a sudden host of Oretani and Vettones. He turns his own horse against the pursuit to draw it away from his sons, and rides into the swollen river, and the water takes him. The Thunderbolt is quenched saving Hannibal and Hasdrubal, who live because their father chose the flood. Hannibal is eighteen. The oath now has no keeper but himself.

stops.name: New Carthage: Qart Hadasht of Hasdrubal, master of horse
stops.campa: Hasdrubal the Handsome, his sister's husband, builds a second Carthage on the lagoon: one gate to the land, silver mines at its back, the finest harbor of Iberia. Hannibal, come of age, commands the cavalry. The canon says no officer matched him: boldest in danger, coolest inside it; no toil could weary the body nor break the spirit; heat and cold alike endured. The army begins to look at him the way it once looked at his father.

stops.name: New Carthage, acclaimed general at twenty-six
stops.campa: A Celtic slave's knife takes Hasdrubal, and the army does not wait for Carthage: the soldiers carry Hannibal to the headquarters tent and hail him general with one shout. He is twenty-six. The old campaigners weep, for they say Hamilcar is given back to them young: the same fire in the face, the same set of the eye. Carthage confirms what the camp has already sworn. The boy of the altar now holds the sword of the west.

stops.name: Althaea, the Olcades broken
stops.campa: His first campaign as general: he falls on the Olcades of the upper country, storms Althaea their strongest town, and the rest submit before the season turns. Tribute and levies flow to New Carthage. The canon notes the method that will empty Italy of certainty: speed before rumor, terror before speed, and generosity the moment the sword is sheathed. He winters rich, paying the army in full and something over.

stops.name: Castulo, the marriage of Imilce
stops.campa: At Castulo of the silver country, chief city of the Oretani, Hannibal takes an Iberian bride: Imilce, daughter of the town's great house. The tradition, which the poets carry, gives her a Greek descent and a son she will carry back to Carthage when the war calls her husband away. The marriage binds the mining heart of Iberia to the Barcids by blood. Of all his bonds, this one the canon barely allows him; the war eats even his household out of the record.

stops.name: Helmantica (Salamanca), the Vaccaei and the women of the town
stops.campa: He drives north across the plateau farther than any Carthaginian has marched and takes Helmantica of the Vaccaei. The town surrenders, then breaks faith; and its women, allowed to walk out unarmed, carry the men's swords beneath their cloaks and put them back in their husbands' hands beyond the gates: a treachery so brave that Hannibal, retaking them, gives the women their freedom and their praise. Arbucala falls next after a long siege. The plateau learns his name.

stops.name: The Tagus ford, the Carpetani drowned
stops.campa: Returning laden with spoil, he is caught by the gathered nations: Carpetani with the fugitives of the Olcades and Vaccaei, a hundred thousand as the canon counts them. He refuses battle, slips across the Tagus by night, and stakes the far bank. When the host wades in, his horsemen ride them down in the stream and forty elephants trample the shallows; then he recrosses and breaks what remains. The river runs bodies. After the Tagus, no people south of the Ebro dares the field against him.
